query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a real-time machine learning–based closed-loop control system that dynamically modulates laser power during LPBF of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy components will reduce melt-pool instabilities and residual stress buildup, thereby improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while simultaneously reducing fabrication-induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) produced by conventional LPBF with fixed parameter settings, exhibiting porosity, dimensional deviations, and residual stresses.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a machine learning–based closed-loop control system for dynamic laser power modulation using in-situ sensor feedback during the LPBF process.
generation.conditions: Standard laser powder bed fusion processing conditions (typical laser power, scanning speeds, inert gas atmosphere, and powder characteristics) under which CoCrFeMnNi components are fabricated for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamically adjusted laser energy input stabilizes the melt pool and minimizes rapid thermal gradients, reducing the formation and propagation of porosity and residual stresses.
generation.mechanism: Real-time sensing of melt-pool characteristics (e.g., temperature, bead geometry) feeds into a machine learning model that predicts optimal laser power adjustments, thereby controlling melt-pool dynamics and solidification behavior to achieve tighter dimensional tolerances and enhanced mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated with the closed-loop control system are expected to exhibit a notable reduction in dimensional deviations (e.g., improved precision by reducing geometrical errors) and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher strength and lower defect density) compared to those produced using conventional fixed parameters.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy components produced under conventional, static LPBF settings with inherent porosity, dimensional inaccuracies, and residual stresses.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within standard LPBF operational windows; however, its performance under extreme parameter deviations or with significantly different powder characteristics remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in dimensional precision and mechanical properties is uncertain and may vary with the quality of in-situ sensing, machine learning model accuracy, and process-specific variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment wherein one set of high-entropy alloy components is produced under standard fixed-parameter LPBF conditions (control group) and another set is fabricated using the real-time machine learning–based closed-loop laser power modulation system (experimental group). Both groups should be fabricated under otherwise identical conditions to isolate the effect of the intervention.
measurements: Quantitative dimensional analysis using coordinate measuring machines to assess geometric deviations.
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile strength, hardness measurements) to evaluate improvements in mechanical integrity.
Defect density assessment via microscopy (e.g., SEM imaging) to quantify porosity and other fabrication-induced defects.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision (e.g., <5% reduction in deviation) and mechanical properties (e.g., <10% improvement in strength or a non-significant reduction in defect density) compared to the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material. decision.trend: Early studies in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys focused on adjusting fixed processing parameters—such as laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing—to optimize microstructural features and mechanical properties. Investigations (e.g., PMC7229066, PMC8201384, PMC9229239) revealed that although controlled energy input and refined grain structures can yield improved strength and hardness, the inherent trade‐offs between porosity, melt‐pool instabilities, and residual stress have not been simultaneously resolved. As the field advanced, researchers began exploring the interplay between process dynamics and in-situ defect formation, noting that conventional parameter sweeps alone cannot fully mitigate dimensional deviations alongside mechanical degradation.
decision.unsolved: A single, integrated intervention to concurrently enhance dimensional precision, mechanical integrity, and reduce fabrication-induced defects remains unaddressed. Current methods optimize individual attributes but are unable to adapt dynamically during fabrication to control melt-pool behavior and residual stress formation.
decision.lever: real-time, machine learning–based closed-loop control for dynamic laser power modulation
decision.why: Leveraging machine learning for in-situ sensing and adaptive control directly follows the trend of moving beyond static parameter tuning. This intervention offers a single, process-integrated solution that can dynamically adjust key parameters (e.g., laser energy input) to stabilize the melt pool and minimize defects, thereby improving both dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity under standard laser powder bed fusion conditions.
